verified_claims_summary: Upshaw et al. (2022) did study 73 college students using a Navon letter task with smartphone-related and control sounds. After exclusions, behavioral analyses included 69 participants and ERP analyses included 54. Responses were significantly slower with smartphone sounds, and N2 ERP amplitude was significantly larger in that condition. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0277220))

The first study used a generic smartphone-vibration notification sound delivered through earphones; the article's description as a notification sound and its statement that participants did not inspect or touch a phone are consistent with the experimental setup. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0277220))

Skowronek et al. (2023) initially recruited 49 students and analyzed 42 after exclusions. Participants were assigned to a condition with a switched-off, screen-covered phone on the desk or a switched-off phone outside the room. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36256-4))

The reported attention-performance means of 99.71 with the phone present and 108.95 without it are exact. The study also found lower work-speed scores with the phone present, 98.48 versus 108.57. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36256-4))

The Pew Research Center figures are accurate: 72% of U.S. teens said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications as soon as they woke up, and 56% associated not having their cellphone with at least one of anxiety, loneliness or upset. ([pewresearch.org](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2018/08/22/how-teens-and-parents-navigate-screen-time-and-device-distractions/))
sources: PLOS ONE article by Upshaw, Stevens, Ganis and Zabelina (2022). ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0277220))
Scientific Reports article by Skowronek, Seifert and Lindberg (2023). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36256-4))
Pew Research Center report published August 22, 2018. ([pewresearch.org](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2018/08/22/how-teens-and-parents-navigate-screen-time-and-device-distractions/))
result.notes: 記事は研究結果を概ね正確に要約している。なお、最初の研究は実際の着信通知ではなく、一般化されたスマートフォン振動音をイヤホンで提示した実験であり、2番目の研究は小規模なオンライン実験だった。しかし、記事は因果関係や一般化を一定程度慎重に表現しており、判定を下げる明確な矛盾や重要な未確認主張はない。
